spike_statement_verdict: The headline claim (1913 state win, 1921 city title, boardwalk groundbreaking) is carried by H053, H055, H063. It holds. Wording issues are in later sections.

blocking.claim: Two other stories do not hold up as the source of the name. ... Later accounts say the 1645 purchase of southern Brooklyn was paid for with a gun, a blanket and a kettle. The deed itself did not record the goods.
blocking.problem: The 1645 purchase/gun-blanket-kettle story is not a name-origin story in any source. H010 says only 'the goods were not recorded in the deed, but later accounts mention a gun, a blanket, and a kettle.' Calling it a story that 'does not hold up as the source of the name' invents a claim no source makes. Only Colman (H008) is a debunked name theory ('nothing connects him with the name'). H010 is also medium confidence.
blocking.evidence: H010 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coney_Island 'the goods were not recorded in the deed, but later accounts mention a gun, a blanket, and a kettle'; H008 https://www.wordorigins.org/big-list-entries/coney-coney-island 'colman did indeed die on coney island, but nothing connects him with the name'
blocking.fix: Replace the whole paragraph beginning 'Two other stories' with: 'One other story does not hold up. John Colman, a crewman of Henry Hudson, did die on Coney Island in 1609, but nothing ties him to the name.'

blocking.where: spoke.history sections[4].body (How did the fenced beach become public?), last paragraph
blocking.claim: Robert Moses thought the job had been done badly. Parks took over the boardwalk in 1938. Moses said that when the city took over Coney Island in 1937, it had only about 50 acres ...
blocking.problem: Overstatement past the quote. H075's quote is 'these beaches and boardwalks were never properly planned, and cannot under present conditions be properly maintained and operated': a general remark about city beaches and boardwalks, not a verdict that the 1921-23 Coney job was done badly. The 50-acre/high-tide remarks (P019) describe the beach Moses inherited in 1937, from a 1954-era speech, and are not a judgment of the boardwalk project. Also the 1937 'took over' wording sits right after the 1921 city-title story with no explanation.
blocking.evidence: H075 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riegelmann_Boardwalk 'these beaches and boardwalks were never properly planned, and cannot under present conditions be properly maintained and operated'; P019 https://wnyc.org/story/electric-eels-bunking-tigers-itinerant-new-york-aquarium/ 'often at high tide there was no beach at all.'
blocking.fix: Replace the last paragraph with: 'Parks took over the boardwalk in 1938. Wikipedia quotes Robert Moses saying that city beaches and boardwalks “were never properly planned.” In a 1950s speech, Moses said that when the city took over Coney Island in 1937, it had only about 50 acres of shrinking, overcrowded beach. “Often at high tide there was no beach at all,” he said.'

blocking.claim: In 2013 the Army Corps of Engineers placed about 580,000 cubic yards of sand on the beach. The Corps says the raised beach avoided an estimated $494 million in damage during Sandy.
blocking.problem: Order implies the 2013 sand (placed after Sandy, October 2012) prevented Sandy damage. P047 says the 2013 sand restored the authorized design; P048/P049 say the already-elevated beach limited damage in the storm. The page also omits that the same source says the surge pushed sand and water over the boardwalk and the beach lost 600,000 cubic yards (P046).
blocking.evidence: P047/P046/P048/P049 https://magazines.marinelink.com/Magazines/MarineTechnology/202307/page/41: 'in 2013, approximately 580,000 cubic yards of sand'; 'coney island beach lost 600,000 cubic yards of sand'; 'avoided an estimated $494 million in damages'; 'hurricane sandy's surge pushed sand and water up and over'
blocking.fix: Replace the three sentences with: 'Hurricane Sandy hit in October 2012. The Army Corps of Engineers says the elevated beach avoided an estimated $494 million in damage to houses and structures during the storm. Marine Technology Reporter says the surge also pushed sand and water over the boardwalk, and the beach lost 600,000 cubic yards of sand. In 2013 the Corps placed about 580,000 cubic yards of sand to restore the beach's authorized design.' Add P046, P049 to fact_ids.

blocking.claim: A draft $52 billion Army Corps flood plan, released in September 2022, would raise the boardwalk five feet with a concrete walkway that acts as a surge barrier. It aimed to start building in 2030.
blocking.problem: A reader will take $52 billion as the Coney Island price. P057's source calls it 'the proposed $52 billion plan for new york and parts of new jersey' (whole region). The source also hedges the design: 'what appears to be a wide concrete walkway', and the 2030 start comes from one 2022 post (P061, medium).
blocking.evidence: P057 https://www.coneyislandhistory.org/node/10607 'the proposed $52 billion plan for new york and parts of new jersey'; P058 https://www.coneyislandhistory.org/node/10729 'the boardwalk would be raised five feet by adding what appears to be a wide concrete walkway'; P061 'the plan will be finalized in two years, and construction begins in 2030.'
blocking.fix: Replace those two sentences with: 'In September 2022 the Army Corps released a draft flood plan for New York and parts of New Jersey. The plan is priced at $52 billion for the whole region. The Coney Island History Project says it would raise the boardwalk five feet with what appears to be a wide concrete walkway that acts as a surge barrier. A 2022 post from the History Project says construction would begin in 2030.' Keep the next sentence 'This page found no source on its status after 2023.'
